- When sentiment is consistently positive (≥ 0.3) over recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast by 2–5% for next period.
- When sentiment is negative (≤ -0.2), model often underestimates; adjust upward by 3–7% if recent price is trending up.
- If model shows sharp upward spike followed by forecast overshoot, apply “lag correction”: subtract 1–3% from forecast 2–3 periods after spike.
- If true outcome shows strong mean reversion (price drops sharply after peak), model often fails to correct; reduce forecast peak by 5–10% if sentiment is neutral or slightly negative.
- For 30-day horizon, model tends to overfit recent volatility; if sentiment is volatile or mixed, smooth forecast by averaging last 5–7 days’ values.
- If sentiment history shows repeated low values (e.g., < 0.1) and price is rising, model may underestimate; add 2–4% to forecast if sentiment is below 0.2 and price is trending up.
- If model forecast is consistently higher than true outcome by > 3% over 3–5 periods, apply “sentiment-weighted decay”: reduce forecast by 0.5–1.5% per period if sentiment is weak or negative.
